title: Playing to Win, Not Just Survive: Lessons from University Leaders
author: Michael B. Horn
summary: Michael Horn draws leadership lessons from two recent episodes of his Future U. podcast with Jeff Selingo, both about university presidents who refuse to manage for survival alone. Melik Khoury of Unity Environmental University argues that governance structures often serve the people who work in an institution rather than its students, and describes spending two and a half years replacing consensus decision making with clear role scope and authority. The result, Horn notes, is a school that grew from small and struggling to roughly 10,000 students. Beong Soo-Kim of USC explains the 'big swings' he plans, chiefly a practicum requirement for every engineering student with faculty supervision and academic criteria, so that immersive learning is substantive rather than decorative. Horn closes by arguing that disruptive innovation theory still explains how different organizations respond to AI. The piece is a curated commentary on the podcasts rather than a full argument, and sits in Leadership because its core subject is how presidents lead institutional change.
points: Khoury's central claim is that tradition gets mistaken for regulation, so leaders must test which governance habits actually serve today's students.
Change at Unity began with the board of trustees and then moved to faculty, staff and students, aligning governance with the mission and what the university can afford to be.
Replacing consensus voting with 'collaboration and engagement with a decision maker' gave deans and directors real authority and took two and a half years to build.
USC's engineering practicum rule shows a big swing done with guardrails: experiences must be substantive, faculty supervised and tied to academic criteria.
Horn's observation that peers ask Khoury how he survived as president, not how he implemented change, captures the survival mindset he wants leaders to drop.
quotes: We all kind of just assumed that what was tradition was regulation. We all assumed that what is doctrine if you will, what is somehow the only way to do education.

We are all trying to do the same things, but we don’t serve the same audience. So for me, it’s like the frog that survived the boiling water and got to leap out and now looking in and saying, wait a second. I could be part of the problem.

But he did explain the importance of starting with the board of trustees and then working with faculty, staff, and students to clarify and rethink governance so that it aligns with the institution’s mission and the kind of university it can afford to be.

So we worked two and a half years on something called role scope and authority where every dean, every director, when we brought people into a room, they got the same collaboration and engagement as they would in a regular institution, but they got to make a decision instead of getting a vote.
Throughout this season, Jeff Selingo has lamented that far too many university presidents are trying not to lose rather than playing to win.
The idea that you would not practice it as part of your education is almost a foreign idea to engineering.
Ian’s point was that hands-on experiences don’t just help students apply what they’ve learned in the classroom. They can also make the classroom learning more meaningful.
I’d argue that these are more relevant than ever—and have been quite helpful in understanding the different responses of different organizations in the AI era.
